title: 1974: free association among early musicians, and later prejudice
summary: Howard and Callender say prejudice among musicians came later; Howard says rednecks at the beach booed musicians, and he got by as a gentleman.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. What was the feeling at that time, I mean with the black and the white, you know, playing together in a ballroom?
Joke fan ... (IN French) (Unintelligible) You know what that means?
You'd better explain that one to me.
(Unintelligible). Oh, that's a French word. It means good.
It worked good as long as the musicians
wanted to?
Well, didn't nobody object to it or nothing.
And so Rudy Wiedoff was actually --
A very nice guy.
a guy who encouraged the blacks and whites (Unintelligible) to --
He didn't encourage them to do nothing.
But I mean knowing somebody like you he would invite you to play with the group.
Yeah, he'd invite me and tell me he was going to play someplace and I'd just go.
Good.

During that period, Mr. Paul, there wasn't much to there wasn't such a thing as prejudice among musicians. That started later, about 1921, when the segregation laws started. Prior to that time it was the words you used. Free association.
Yeah, free association. Just go on and play.
That was nice. And then later on, you're right, it got the point where --
That happened later.
Yeah, real late. It happened real late.
You saw a lot of these changes take place, didn't you?
Oh, yes.
Yeah.
I'm trying to think of a situation that would take care of this, like this -- you start to playing, working with somebody and, "We don't them niggers up here." Oh, down at the --
On Main Street?
You don't remember a name Harry Souther, do you?
What's that name again?
Souther. Some people called it Sowther, but it wasn't Sowther. It was Souther.
Sounds familiar, but I couldn't tell you.
A trombone player.
I've read that name somewhere.
Huh?
I've read that name.
Yeah. He was a trombone player.
Yeah. I've read the name, yeah.
Harry Souther.

Yeah, that's his name. Ernest Coycault. They had a band. We used to go down to the beach and play. And sometimes those rednecks down there didn't want you down there, and they didn't want you down there they'd
just boo you out of the place, you know.
And a lot of the time that would start from the patrons, the people, rather than the management? You know what I mean?
It'd start from the musicians.
Oh, the musicians would start it.
Yeah. Instead of the patrons. They started that.
I just wondered where -- you know, because everybody blames everybody else is what I'm saying. But the musicians didn't want you there.

They didn't want you there. Some of them didn't and some of them did. Most all of them did. Most all of them would treat you very nice that knew you. I never had no trouble with anybody, playing. But I think it was just all on what type of a person it was. I was always -- excuse me for saying like this -- I'm speaking of myself now -- but I was always a very unassuming person. I never got forward with nobody. I never got angry with anybody. I never called people out their names. I didn't swear. I didn't do none of those things. I always tried to be a gentleman with everybody. And that way it got me by lots of places.
